question: Explain what Docker is and how a container differs from a traditional virtual machine.

key_points: A container packages an application with its dependencies (libraries, runtime) into a portable, isolated unit that runs consistently across environments
Containers share the host machine's OS kernel, using kernel features (namespaces, cgroups) for isolation, rather than virtualizing hardware
A VM virtualizes an entire machine including its own full OS kernel, making it heavier (more memory/disk, slower to boot) but more strongly isolated
Explains containers start in seconds/milliseconds versus a VM's much slower boot, and have much smaller image sizes since they don't bundle a full OS
Notes containers and VMs are often combined in practice: containers running on VM-based cloud instances for an extra isolation layer
reference_solution.sample_answer: A Docker container packages an application together with everything it needs to run — libraries, dependencies, runtime — into one portable image that behaves the same way regardless of where it's deployed. Containers share the host machine's OS kernel, using Linux kernel features like namespaces and cgroups to isolate processes, filesystems, and resource usage from each other, rather than virtualizing hardware. A traditional VM instead virtualizes an entire machine, including its own separate OS kernel, which gives stronger isolation but makes VMs much heavier — more memory and disk usage, and boot times measured in tens of seconds versus a container starting in milliseconds. In practice, both are often combined: containers running on top of VM-based cloud instances for an extra layer of isolation.

follow_up_hint: Ask what cgroups and namespaces specifically do to isolate a container's resource usage and view of the system.

question: Explain the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container, and what a Dockerfile does.

key_points: A Docker image is a read-only, immutable template — the filesystem and configuration needed to run an application
A container is a running (or stopped) instance of an image, with its own writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers
You can run multiple independent containers from the exact same image
A Dockerfile is a text file of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD, etc.) describing how to build an image step by step, layer by layer
Explains layer caching: each Dockerfile instruction creates a cacheable layer, so unchanged early steps (e.g. installing dependencies) don't need to be re-executed on every build
reference_solution.sample_answer: A Docker image is an immutable, read-only template containing everything needed to run an application — think of it like a class. A container is a running instance created from that image — like an object instantiated from that class — with its own thin writable layer on top of the image's read-only layers, and you can run many independent containers from the same image simultaneously. A Dockerfile is the recipe for building an image: a sequence of instructions like FROM (base image), COPY (add files), RUN (execute a build step), and CMD (default command when the container starts). Each instruction produces a cacheable layer, so if you change only your application code near the end of the Dockerfile, earlier layers like dependency installation can be reused from cache instead of rerunning.

follow_up_hint: Ask how they'd order Dockerfile instructions to maximize build-cache reuse for a typical Node.js or Python app.

question: Explain what Kubernetes is and what problem it solves that plain Docker doesn't address by itself.

key_points: Docker packages and runs individual containers, but doesn't natively handle running many containers reliably across a cluster of machines
Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform: it schedules containers across a cluster of nodes, restarts failed containers, and handles scaling
Provides declarative configuration: you describe the desired state (e.g. '5 replicas of this service'), and Kubernetes continuously works to match reality to that desired state
Handles service discovery and load balancing between containers automatically, plus rolling updates and rollbacks with minimal downtime
Explains this solves problems like: what happens when a container crashes, how to scale to handle more traffic, and how services find each other across many dynamically placed containers
reference_solution.sample_answer: Docker handles building and running individual containers, but running a real application often means many containers across many machines that need to be scheduled, restarted on failure, scaled up and down, and able to find and talk to each other — Docker alone doesn't manage any of that at a cluster level. Kubernetes is a container orchestration platform that does exactly this: you declare the desired state, like 'run 5 replicas of this service', and Kubernetes continuously reconciles the actual cluster state to match, automatically rescheduling a container if a node fails, load-balancing traffic across replicas via built-in service discovery, and performing rolling updates so you can deploy a new version with minimal or zero downtime.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to explain what a Kubernetes Pod is and why it's the smallest deployable unit rather than a single container directly.

question: Explain the core Kubernetes objects: Pod, Deployment, and Service, and how they relate to each other.

key_points: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more tightly coupled containers sharing the same network namespace and storage volumes
A Deployment manages a set of identical Pod replicas, handling rolling updates, rollbacks, and self-healing (recreating Pods that die)
A Service provides a stable network endpoint (a fixed virtual IP/DNS name) that load-balances traffic across the current set of matching Pods, even as Pods are created/destroyed and get new IPs
Explains why Pods have ephemeral IPs and why a Service is needed to give consumers a stable way to reach them
Gives the relationship: a Deployment creates and manages Pods; a Service selects and routes to Pods (often those managed by a Deployment) via label selectors
reference_solution.sample_answer: A Pod is Kubernetes' smallest deployable unit — usually one container, sometimes a few tightly coupled ones, sharing a network namespace and storage. A Deployment manages a desired number of identical Pod replicas, handling rolling out new versions gradually, rolling back on failure, and recreating Pods automatically if they crash or their node fails. Pods are ephemeral though — they can be destroyed and recreated with a brand new IP address at any time — so a Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name that automatically load-balances traffic across whichever Pods currently match its label selector, regardless of how many times those underlying Pods have been replaced. In short: a Deployment ensures the right Pods exist, and a Service provides a stable way for other things to reach them.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to explain how a Service's label selector actually determines which Pods it routes traffic to.

question: Explain what a CI/CD pipeline is, distinguishing continuous integration from continuous delivery/deployment.

key_points: Continuous Integration: developers merge code changes frequently, each triggering an automated build and test run to catch integration issues early
Continuous Delivery: every change that passes CI is automatically prepared into a releasable artifact, ready to deploy at any time, typically with a manual approval gate before production
Continuous Deployment: goes one step further, automatically deploying every change that passes all checks straight to production with no manual gate
Explains the value: catching bugs early (CI), and reducing the risk/effort of releasing (CD) by making releases small, frequent, and routine rather than large and risky
Names common tooling examples (e.g. GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI) without needing deep tool-specific detail
reference_solution.sample_answer: Continuous Integration means developers merge their changes frequently, and each merge automatically triggers a build and test run, catching integration problems (broken builds, failing tests) quickly rather than discovering them much later. Continuous Delivery extends this: every change that passes CI is automatically packaged into a deployable artifact and is always in a release-ready state, though an actual production deploy might still require a manual approval step. Continuous Deployment goes further still, automatically deploying every passing change straight to production with no manual gate at all. Together these practices make releases small, frequent, and low-risk, versus infrequent, large, high-risk releases — implemented via tools like GitHub Actions, Jenkins, or GitLab CI.

follow_up_hint: Ask what safeguards (e.g. automated smoke tests, canary deploys, feature flags) they'd want in place before trusting full continuous deployment to production.

question: Explain blue-green deployment and canary deployment strategies, and the trade-offs between them.

key_points: Blue-green: runs two identical full environments (blue = current, green = new); traffic is switched all at once from blue to green after the new version is verified
Blue-green allows near-instant rollback (switch traffic back to blue) but requires running two full production-scale environments simultaneously, doubling resource cost during the switch
Canary: gradually shifts a small percentage of real traffic to the new version, monitoring for errors before progressively increasing the percentage

Canary limits the blast radius of a bad deploy to a small fraction of users, but requires good monitoring/metrics to actually detect problems during the gradual rollout, and is more complex to orchestrate
Notes both aim to reduce deployment risk, just via different trade-offs between simplicity/speed of rollback (blue-green) and blast-radius limitation (canary)
reference_solution.sample_answer: Blue-green deployment keeps two full, identical environments — the current 'blue' version serving live traffic, and a new 'green' version deployed alongside it. Once green is verified, traffic is switched over all at once, and rollback is just switching back to blue instantly if something's wrong — but this requires running two full production-scale environments simultaneously, which is expensive. Canary deployment instead gradually shifts a small percentage of real traffic (e.g. 5%) to the new version, closely monitoring error rates and other metrics, and only increases that percentage if things look healthy. Canary limits how many users are affected by a bad deploy, but requires solid real-time monitoring to actually catch problems during the gradual rollout, and is generally more complex to set up and coordinate than an all-at-once blue-green switch.

follow_up_hint: Ask them what specific metrics they'd monitor during a canary rollout to decide whether to proceed, pause, or roll back.

question: Explain Infrastructure as Code (IaC), and why it's preferred over manually configuring servers through a cloud console.

key_points: IaC defines infrastructure (servers, networks, databases) in version-controlled configuration files rather than manual point-and-click setup
Benefits: repeatability (the same config reliably produces the same environment every time), and reviewability (infrastructure changes go through the same PR/review process as code)
Enables disaster recovery: a lost environment can be recreated exactly from the code, rather than relying on someone remembering manual steps that were taken
Explains 'declarative' IaC tools (like Terraform) where you describe the desired end state, versus manual changes which can drift and become undocumented over time ('configuration drift')
Notes IaC also enables easily spinning up identical staging/dev environments matching production
reference_solution.sample_answer: Infrastructure as Code means defining servers, networks, and other infrastructure in version-controlled configuration files, applied by a tool, rather than manually clicking through a cloud console. This gives repeatability — the exact same configuration reliably produces the exact same environment every time — and lets infrastructure changes go through the same code review process as application code. It also makes disaster recovery realistic: if an environment is lost, it can be recreated exactly from the code rather than depending on someone's memory of the manual steps originally taken. Declarative tools like Terraform let you describe the desired end state and have the tool figure out what changes to make, avoiding the 'configuration drift' problem where manually-managed infrastructure slowly diverges from what anyone actually knows or documented.

follow_up_hint: Ask them what 'configuration drift' means concretely and how IaC with a tool like Terraform detects and corrects it.

question: Explain what a load balancer health check is, and how a Kubernetes readiness probe differs from a liveness probe.

key_points: A health check periodically pings an instance to determine whether it should keep receiving traffic
A liveness probe checks whether a container is still running correctly at all — if it fails repeatedly, Kubernetes kills and restarts the container

A readiness probe checks whether a container is currently ready to accept traffic — if it fails, Kubernetes stops sending it new requests (removes it from the Service's endpoints) WITHOUT restarting it

Gives a concrete distinction: an app that's alive but temporarily overloaded or still warming up a cache should fail readiness (stop getting new traffic) but not liveness (don't restart it, that wouldn't help)
Explains getting these probes wrong (e.g. too aggressive liveness checks) can cause unnecessary restart loops for an app that's just temporarily slow
reference_solution.sample_answer: A health check periodically verifies whether an instance should keep receiving live traffic. In Kubernetes specifically, a liveness probe checks whether the container is fundamentally still functioning — if it keeps failing, Kubernetes assumes the process is stuck or broken and restarts the container. A readiness probe checks whether the container is currently able to handle requests well — if it fails, Kubernetes just stops routing new traffic to it via the Service, without restarting it. The distinction matters concretely: an app that's alive but still warming up a cache, or briefly overloaded, should fail its readiness check (temporarily pulled from traffic) but must NOT fail liveness, since restarting it wouldn't actually help and would just cause a pointless restart loop.

follow_up_hint: Ask them to describe a real incident scenario where a misconfigured liveness probe caused a restart loop that made an outage worse, not better.

question: Explain the difference between horizontal pod autoscaling and cluster autoscaling in Kubernetes.

key_points: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling (HPA) adjusts the NUMBER of Pod replicas for a given workload based on observed metrics (e.g. CPU/memory usage, or custom metrics like request rate)
Cluster Autoscaling adjusts the number of underlying NODES (machines) in the cluster, adding nodes when Pods can't be scheduled due to insufficient capacity, and removing underutilized nodes
Explains the two typically work together: HPA scales Pods up, which may then require Cluster Autoscaler to add nodes if there isn't room to schedule the new Pods on existing nodes
Notes HPA operates at the application/workload level; Cluster Autoscaler operates at the infrastructure level
Mentions Vertical Pod Autoscaling as a related but distinct concept, adjusting a Pod's resource requests/limits rather than replica count
reference_solution.sample_answer: Horizontal Pod Autoscaling changes how many replicas of a Pod are running, based on metrics like CPU usage or a custom application metric — more load means more replicas, within configured min/max bounds. Cluster Autoscaling operates one level down, at the infrastructure layer: it adds new nodes (machines) to the cluster when there isn't enough capacity to schedule newly needed Pods, and removes nodes that have become underutilized. The two usually work together: if HPA decides it needs 10 more replicas but the existing nodes don't have room, Cluster Autoscaler kicks in to provision new nodes so those Pods can actually be scheduled. There's also Vertical Pod Autoscaling, a related but distinct mechanism that instead adjusts a Pod's own CPU/memory requests and limits rather than changing how many replicas exist.

follow_up_hint: Ask what happens if HPA wants to scale up but Cluster Autoscaler can't provision new nodes fast enough — how does that affect the application?

question: What are the main differences between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS cloud service models, with an example of each?

key_points: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): provides raw compute, storage, and networking; the user manages the OS, runtime, and application, e.g. AWS EC2
PaaS (Platform as a Service): provides a managed runtime/platform; the user just deploys application code without managing the underlying OS/servers, e.g. Heroku or AWS Elastic Beanstalk
SaaS (Software as a Service): a fully finished application delivered over the internet, with no infrastructure or platform management by the user at all, e.g. Gmail or Salesforce
Explains the trend of decreasing user responsibility (and decreasing flexibility) as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS
Gives a clear, distinct real-world example for each tier
reference_solution.sample_answer: IaaS gives you raw virtualized infrastructure — compute, storage, networking — and you're responsible for everything above that, including the OS and runtime; AWS EC2 is a classic example. PaaS abstracts away the OS and server management entirely — you just deploy your application code, and the platform handles running, scaling, and patching the underlying environment; Heroku or AWS Elastic Beanstalk fit here. SaaS is a complete, ready-to-use application delivered over the internet with no infrastructure or platform concerns for the user at all, like Gmail or Salesforce. Moving from IaaS to SaaS trades away flexibility and control in exchange for less operational responsibility.

follow_up_hint: Ask them where a managed database service like AWS RDS fits on this spectrum, and why it's a bit of a hybrid.
